1: # Agent Deck
2: 
3: [![VS Code Marketplace](https://img.shields.io/visual-studio-marketplace/v/nvitlam.agent-deck?label=VS%20Code%20Marketplace)](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=nvitlam.agent-deck)
4: 
5: A **read-only** VS Code extension that renders live Claude Code session topology — subagent trees,
6: in-flight tool calls, token and cost totals — by observing Claude Code's exhaust. It never wraps,
7: proxies, launches, or configures Claude Code.
8: 
9: > **Claude Code compatibility** — anchor `2.1.246`, accepts `2.0.x` to `2.2.x`, refuses on
10: > structural change, not on patch number. See [Claude Code version window](#claude-code-version-window).
11: >
12: > This badge is text, not a remote image: a project whose selling point is zero egress should not
13: > make its own README phone home to a badge service to render.
14: 
15: ---
16: 
17: ![Agent Deck](media/screenshot-deck.png)
18: 
19: ## Read-only by design
20: 
21: Agent Deck observes. It never acts.
22: 
23: - It reads Claude Code's session JSONL and listens for hook events. That is all.
24: - It never wraps, proxies, launches or configures Claude Code.
25: - It never writes to `~/.claude`, to Claude Code settings, or to your session
26:   files. Installing the hooks is a manual paste block you control, below.
27: - Zero network egress. The only socket it opens is an HTTP listener bound to
28:   `127.0.0.1`, which is how the hooks reach it. Non-loopback requests are
29:   dropped.
30: - No telemetry, no analytics, no CDN. Every asset the panel renders is local,
31:   enforced by a strict Content-Security-Policy.
32: 
33: All state lives in memory and is discarded when the window closes.
34: 
35: ## Features
36: 
37: **The deck** - every live session at a glance, breathing while it works.
38: 
39: ![The deck](media/screenshot-deck.png)
40: 
41: **Agent topology** - the main agent as a nucleus, tool calls as chronological
42: dots, and subagents joined by filaments to the exact `tool_use` block that
43: spawned them. That join is a primary key, not a guess.
44: 
45: ![Agent topology](media/screenshot-topology.png)
46: 
47: **Tool call inspector** - open any node for its payload, truncated with an
48: explicit marker and with thinking blocks dropped at the parse boundary.
49: 
50: ![Tool call inspector](media/screenshot-inspector.png)
51: 
52: ## What it is
53: 
54: Claude Code leaves two kinds of exhaust behind, and Agent Deck reads both without touching either:
55: 
56: | Tap | Source | What it answers |
57: | --- | --- | --- |
58: | **Hooks** | a hook snippet *you* paste into your settings POSTs to a loopback HTTP listener | what is running right now |
59: | **JSONL** | `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/...`, read from local disk | what happened |
60: 
61: The split is deliberate. The hook contract is documented and stable with thin payloads; the session
62: files are undocumented and rich. Keeping them on separate failure paths means a Claude Code schema
63: change degrades the panel instead of killing it.
64: 
65: Everything the extension knows lives in memory in the extension host and is discarded when the
66: window closes. There is no database, no cache file, and nothing is ever written back to Claude Code.
67: 
68: ## Requirements
69: 
70: - **VS Code** `^1.75.0`
71: - **Node** `>=20` on your `PATH` — the hook block below is a `node -e` one-liner, so your Node is
72:   what runs it
73: - **Claude Code** on the `2.x` line, within one minor of the anchor (see below). Patch releases are
74:   read as they come.
75: 
76: ## Install
77: 
78: Install from the VS Code Marketplace - open the **Extensions** view and search for
79: **Agent Deck**, or run:
80: 
81: ```console
82: code --install-extension nvitlam.agent-deck
83: ```
84: 
85: **Then install the hook block below.** It is not optional: without it Agent Deck can still read
86: session transcripts, but nothing tells it what is running right now, so liveness is inferred from
87: file mtime alone.
88: 
89: ## Install the hook (one manual paste)
90: 
91: Content and the tree render from the session files alone. The hook tap is what makes liveness
92: *live* — which agent is running right now, which tool call is in flight.
93: 
94: **Agent Deck never installs this for you and never writes either settings file.** Read-only means
95: read-only, including your configuration. You paste it; you own it.
96: 
97: Paste the `"hooks"` key below into **one** of:
98: 
99: - your project's own `.claude/settings.local.json` — what this repository does, and the choice that
100:   keeps `~/.claude` untouched entirely; or
101: - your user-level `~/.claude/settings.json`, if you would rather have it everywhere.
102: 
103: Both files are JSON objects. Merge the `"hooks"` key into whatever is already there rather than
104: replacing the file.
105: 
106: ```json

1: # CLAUDE.md
2: 
3: This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
4: 
5: ## Current state
6: 
7: > **2026-08-26 — `v0.1.2` is LIVE on the Marketplace. Plan v0.5.0 is running; Phase 0 is the
8: > current phase. `PLAN.md` (the v0.5.0 file) is the contract; the superseded v2 plan is archived
9: > byte-identical at `docs/PLAN-v2.md` and its closed-phase records are never altered.**
10: >
11: > **What shipped, and why it had to.** `v0.1.1` refused every Claude Code session written from
12: > 2026-08-24 onward, on every machine, because its version check capped at `2.1.239` and CC shipped
13: > `2.1.240`. `v0.1.2` stops comparing the patch component, makes the structural fingerprint the only
14: > in-range refusal, and re-anchors on `2.1.246` with two captured corpora. That was **v0.5.0 Phase 1,
15: > pulled forward and released as a hotfix** (gate H1, option (i)); DoD 1.7 is signed at
16: > `docs/evidence/phase-1/OWN-EYES.md`. Do not re-run Phase 1.
17: >
18: > **Where v0.5.0 is.** Phase 0 (this one): archive, fold in the OpenCode branch, housekeeping,
19: > Wave 0. Phase 1 closed. **Phase 2 is a binary GO/NO-GO kill gate** — `node:sqlite` read-only
20: > against a live WAL database *from inside the extension host*, which has never been run there; a
21: > NO-GO kills the OpenCode engine design and the fallback needs a G5 amendment and a user decision.
22: > Phases 3-5 build that engine, 6-7 the tree UI, 8-9 release. **Phase 6 (the `docs/ui/design.md`
23: > design track) runs in parallel and is authored by the user in Claude.ai; Phase 7 may not dispatch

# Skill: phase

# Execute a phase (orchestrator protocol)

You are the ORCHESTRATOR. You do not write implementation code yourself in this
mode. You decompose, dispatch, monitor, verify, and merge. Workers do the work.

## Phase 0 — Load, read, gate
1. Read PLAN.md. Identify the target phase number (from the user's argument, or
   the first phase not marked complete).
2. **Kickoff reading.** If the phase section declares a `**Kickoff reading**` list,
   read every entry in the listed order before extracting anything else. The list is
   the phase's own declaration of what its executor must understand — skipping an
   entry is a process failure, recorded as a deviation in the handoff. A phase
   section without the list gets the default: this file's Grounding Contract +
   Swarm Protocol, the phase section, and the current HANDOVER.md.
3. **Re-measure, do not read.** The plan's "Status as of planning" block — and
   HANDOVER/CLAUDE state claims generally — are snapshots that can be stale: this
   repo has closed phases, changed visibility, and rewritten history between
   planning and dispatch. Before presenting open questions, run the phase's
   declared re-measurement commands (default: `git log --oneline -5`,
   `git status --short`, `node scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs`) and compare them with
   the documents. If measurement disagrees with a document, the measurement wins
   and the discrepancy is raised at the gate — it is NOT patched into the
   documents mid-phase; the handoff fixes documents.
4. Extract: the phase's Definition of Done (DoD), module list, test
   expectations, and open-question checklist.
5. Present ALL open questions as ONE consolidated checklist, including any
   discrepancy found in step 3 as its own question. STOP and wait for answers.
   Do not dispatch anything until every question is resolved.

## Phase 1 — Decompose into work packages
6. Split the phase into work packages **partitioned by module boundary**.
   Hard rule: no two packages may own the same file. If two modules must touch
   the same file, merge them into one package.
7. For each package record: package ID, owned files/directories, the spec slice
   from PLAN.md relevant to it, the DoD items it satisfies, and its module-level
   test command.
8. Parallelization rules:
   - Packages with no dependency between them → dispatch in parallel.
   - Dependent packages → dispatch in dependency order (parallel within each wave).
   - A package touching fewer than ~3 files is not worth a worker — batch it
     with a neighbor or do it in the final integration step.
   - Cap concurrent implementers at 4 unless the user raises it.
9. Show the user the dispatch plan as a compact table (package → files → DoD
   items → wave). Proceed unless they object.

## Phase 2 — Dispatch the fleet
10. For each package in the current wave, spawn a `phase-implementer` subagent
    in the background. The delegation prompt MUST be self-contained — the worker
    sees nothing of this conversation. Include verbatim:
    - The package's spec slice from PLAN.md
    - The exact list of files it owns (and that it must touch nothing else)
    - The DoD items it is responsible for
    - The module test command it must pass before reporting
    - The required report format (defined in the agent file)
    - The budget law: write all the code first, run its module tests once, fix,
      run again; never run the full suite from a worker
11. While workers run, you may answer user questions but make no code edits.
    Track worker status; the user can watch /tasks.

## Phase 3 — Collect, merge, integrate
12. As each worker reports, check the report against the required format.
    A report missing evidence (test output, file list) is rejected: resume that
    SAME worker via SendMessage with what's missing — do not spawn a fresh one.
13. Workers run in isolated git worktrees. After a wave completes, merge each
    worktree branch into the phase branch. On merge conflict: the package
    partitioning failed — resolve manually in the main session and note the
    boundary violation for /handoff.
14. Perform any small glue/integration edits yourself (imports, wiring,
    config) — this is the only code the orchestrator writes.

## Phase 4 — Verify
15. Spawn `test-runner` to execute the FULL test suite. Do not proceed until it
    reports 100% pass with exact counts. On failures: resume the implementer
    that owns the failing module with the failure output. Repeat until green.
16. Spawn `phase-verifier` with the full DoD checklist. It returns PASS/FAIL
    per item with repo evidence. Any FAIL → route back to the owning
    implementer (resume, don't respawn), then re-verify. Do not self-certify;
    only the verifier's PASS counts.

## Phase 5 — Close
17. Commit on the phase branch with a clear message listing the DoD items
    satisfied and the exact test counts from test-runner's report.
18. Run /handoff. The handoff must supersede stale state documents: HANDOVER.md
    is rewritten for the next phase, and CLAUDE.md's "Current state" is brought
    to the closed phase — a closed phase whose state blocks still open on an
    earlier phase is this repo's most-repeated defect (PLAN's Phase 6 section
    records it against itself), and the verifier is to check for it.

## Failure and escalation rules
- A worker blocked on a spec ambiguity must report BLOCKED, not guess. Surface
  the question to the user, get an answer, resume the worker with it.
- If a worker exceeds its scope (edits an unowned file), discard its worktree,
  respawn with a tightened prompt.
- If the same package fails verification twice after resume, stop the fleet and
  escalate to the user with the verifier's evidence.
- Serial fallback: if the phase is tightly coupled (single module, shared
  state), skip the fleet and implement directly in the main session, then still
  run Phases 4–5 (test-runner + verifier are mandatory regardless).

Welcome to the 1.134 release of Visual Studio Code. This release helps you work across windows, organize related chats side by side, and navigate long conversations faster.

-   [Side-by-side chats](#_grid-layout-for-chats-in-a-session): Arrange related chats and subagent chats in groups for easier comparison.
    
-   [Prompt timeline](#_prompt-timeline): Quickly navigate across prompts and review their file changes.
    
-   [Find in chat](#_find-in-chat): Search for text in the complete conversation with ease.
    
-   [Preview HTML files](#_open-html-files-in-the-integrated-browser-by-default): Preview local HTML files directly in VS Code by making the integrated browser their default editor.
    

Happy Coding!

VS Code is rolling out gradually to all users. Use **Check for Updates** in VS Code to get the latest version immediately.

To try new features as soon as possible, [**download the nightly Insiders build**](https://code.visualstudio.com/insiders), which includes the latest updates as soon as they are available.

## Agents

### Agent host

The agent host lets you connect to the same agent session from multiple VS Code windows. It runs agent harnesses in a dedicated process based on the [Agent Host Protocol](https://microsoft.github.io/agent-host-protocol/) (AHP). The agent host's Copilot agent is powered by the [Copilot SDK](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@github/copilot-sdk), which aligns the agent's behavior and functionality with the Copilot CLI, the standalone GitHub Copilot app, and other Copilot products.

We're actively developing the agent host. The following screenshot shows the `Copilot` harness selected for an agent host in an editor window:

![Screenshot showing the harness dropdown in the editor window.](/assets/updates/1_134/agent-host-harness-dropdown-editor.webp)

You can learn more in our [VS Code Agent Host documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/concepts/agent-host). If you have any feedback or requests, please let us know by [filing an issue](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues).

### Grid layout for chats in a session

Keep related conversations visible by arranging chats in horizontal or vertical groups. Drag chats or subagent chats into a group to compare results or monitor work side by side. VS Code restores the chat-group layout and focus when you return to the session or reload the window.

Create a side chat to open a new conversation beside the current chat.

Drag and drop a subagent chat into a group to view it side by side with the current chat.

You can also Alt+select a chat in the **Chats** picker to open it to the side.

### Improvements to the side pane layout

**Settings**: sessions.layout.singlePaneDetailPanel Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders and workbench.editor.showTabs Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders

The single-pane layout keeps session details and editors in a shared tab bar next to chat. This release makes the layout easier to control:

-   The layout follows the workbench.editor.showTabs Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders setting. Multiple tabs remain visible, while the `single` and `none` values use a compact single-title header.
    
    ![Screenshot showing the compact single-title header in the Agents window.](/assets/updates/1_134/agents-window-single-tab.webp)
    
-   Text file editors use the same header structure as the Changes editor, with file breadcrumbs in the header.
    
-   The side pane keeps its size and visibility when you switch sessions, avoiding unexpected layout shifts.
    

Enable sessions.layout.singlePaneDetailPanel Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders and reload the window to use this layout.

### Prompt timeline

**Setting**: sessions.chatTimeline.display Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders

Long agent sessions can make it difficult to find earlier prompts and identify which ones changed files.

The Agents window includes a timeline in the transcript gutter. Each dot represents one of your prompts, and the highlighted dot marks your current position. Hover over the timeline to view your prompts, then select one to jump to it. For prompts that changed files, the list shows the number of lines added and removed and lets you open the changes directly for review.

Use the sessions.chatTimeline.display Open in VS Code Open in VS Code Insiders setting to show the timeline beside the scrollbar (`ruler`) or hide it (`off`).

## Chat

### Find in chat

Finding information from earlier in a long conversation previously required scrolling through the transcript. Use ⌘F (Windows, Linux Ctrl+F) to search conversations in the Chat view, chat editors, and the Agents window.

Search includes the entire conversation, even content that is not currently rendered on screen. As you move between matches, VS Code scrolls each match into view and expands a collapsed work summary if it contains the match. You can also match case, match whole words, or use regular expressions.

## Editor Experience

### Close other editors from a tab

Keep one editor open without using the tab context menu. Hold Alt to change the close action on each editor tab to **Close Other Editors**, then select the action on the tab you want to keep.

# Server

Interact with opencode server over HTTP.

The `opencode serve` command runs a headless HTTP server that exposes an OpenAPI endpoint that an opencode client can use.

---

### [Usage](#usage)

Terminal window

```
opencode serve [--port <number>] [--hostname <string>] [--cors <origin>]
```

#### [Options](#options)

Flag

Description

Default

`--port`

Port to listen on

`4096`

`--hostname`

Hostname to listen on

`127.0.0.1`

`--mdns`

Enable mDNS discovery

`false`

`--mdns-domain`

Custom domain name for mDNS service

`opencode.local`

`--cors`

Additional browser origins to allow

`[]`

`--cors` can be passed multiple times:

Terminal window

```
opencode serve --cors http://localhost:5173 --cors https://app.example.com
```

---

### [Authentication](#authentication)

Set `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` to protect the server with HTTP basic auth. The username defaults to `opencode`, or set `OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME` to override it. This applies to both `opencode serve` and `opencode web`.

Terminal window

```
OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD=your-password opencode serve
```

---

### [How it works](#how-it-works)

When you run `opencode` it starts a TUI and a server. Where the TUI is the client that talks to the server. The server exposes an OpenAPI 3.1 spec endpoint. This endpoint is also used to generate an [SDK](/docs/sdk).

Tip

Use the opencode server to interact with opencode programmatically.

This architecture lets opencode support multiple clients and allows you to interact with opencode programmatically.

You can run `opencode serve` to start a standalone server. If you have the opencode TUI running, `opencode serve` will start a new server.

---

#### [Connect to an existing server](#connect-to-an-existing-server)

When you start the TUI it randomly assigns a port and hostname. You can instead pass in the `--hostname` and `--port` [flags](/docs/cli). Then use this to connect to its server.

The [`/tui`](#tui) endpoint can be used to drive the TUI through the server. For example, you can prefill or run a prompt. This setup is used by the OpenCode [IDE](/docs/ide) plugins.

---

## [Spec](#spec)

The server publishes an OpenAPI 3.1 spec that can be viewed at:

```
http://<hostname>:<port>/doc
```

For example, `http://localhost:4096/doc`. Use the spec to generate clients or inspect request and response types. Or view it in a Swagger explorer.

---

# Electron Releases

Electron frequently releases major versions alongside every other Chromium release. This document focuses on the release cadence and version support policy.

tip

See the [Electron Versioning](/docs/latest/tutorial/electron-versioning) document for more details on how Electron is versioned.

## Timeline[​](#timeline "Direct link to Timeline")

[Electron's Release Schedule](https://releases.electronjs.org/schedule) lists a schedule of Electron major releases showing key milestones including alpha, beta, and stable release dates, as well as end-of-life dates and dependency versions.

info

Electron's official support policy is the latest 3 stable releases. Our stable release and end-of-life dates are determined by Chromium, and may be subject to change. While we try to keep our planned release and end-of-life dates frequently updated here, future dates may change if affected by upstream scheduling changes, and may not always be accurately reflected.

See [Chromium's public release schedule](https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule) for definitive information about Chromium's scheduled release dates.

Electron's cadence between major version releases is 8 weeks long. Before each major version hits stable, it goes through a four-week **alpha** phase and a four-week **beta** phase.

**Notes:**

-   Alphas are generally less stable than beta releases. The cutoff between the two corresponds to when the underlying Chromium version enters Chrome's Beta channel.
-   The `-alpha.1`, `-beta.1`, and `stable` dates are our solid release dates.
-   We strive for weekly alpha/beta releases, but we often release more than scheduled.
-   All dates are our goals but there may be reasons for adjusting the stable deadline, such as security bugs.

**Historical changes:**

-   Since Electron 5, Electron has been publicizing its release dates ([see blog post](https://www.electronjs.org/blog/electron-5-0-timeline)).
-   Since Electron 6, Electron major versions have been targeting every other Chromium major version. Each Electron stable should happen on the same day as Chrome stable ([see blog post](https://www.electronjs.org/blog/12-week-cadence)).
-   Since Electron 16, Electron has been releasing major versions on an 8-week cadence in accordance to Chrome's change to a 4-week release cadence ([see blog post](https://www.electronjs.org/blog/8-week-cadence)).
-   Electron temporarily extended support for Electron 22 until October 10, 2023, to support an extended end-of-life for Windows 7/8/8.1

## Version support policy[​](#version-support-policy "Direct link to Version support policy")

The latest three *stable* major versions are supported by the Electron team.

For example, if the latest release is 42.1.x, then the 41.0.x as well as the 40.2.x series are supported. We only support the latest minor release for each stable release series. This means that in the case of a security fix, 42.1.x will receive the fix, but we will not release a new version of 42.0.x.

The latest stable release unilaterally receives all fixes from `main`, and the version prior to that receives the vast majority of those fixes as time and bandwidth warrants. The oldest supported release line will receive only security fixes directly.

### Chromium version support[​](#chromium-version-support "Direct link to Chromium version support")

tip

Chromium's public release schedule is [here](https://chromiumdash.appspot.com/schedule).

Electron targets Chromium even-number versions, releasing every 8 weeks in concert with Chromium's 4-week release schedule. For example, Electron 26 uses Chromium 116, while Electron 27 uses Chromium 118.

### Node.js version support[​](#nodejs-version-support "Direct link to Node.js version support")

Electron upgrades its `main` branch to even-number versions of Node.js when they enter Active LTS. The schedule is as follows:

![Releases](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nodejs/Release/main/schedule.svg?sanitize=true)

If Electron has recently updated its `main` branch to a new major version of Node.js, the next stable branch to be cut will be released with the new version.

Stable release lines of Electron will receive minor and patch bumps of Node.js after they are released. Patch bumps to Node.js will be released in patch releases of Electron, and minor bumps to Node.js will result in a minor release of Electron. Security-only release branches will receive security-related changes from Node.js releases, but not the full release.

### Breaking API changes[​](#breaking-api-changes "Direct link to Breaking API changes")

When an API is changed or removed in a way that breaks existing functionality, the previous functionality will be supported for a minimum of two major versions when possible before being removed. For example, if a function takes three arguments, and that number is reduced to two in major version 10, the three-argument version would continue to work until, at minimum, major version 12. Past the minimum two-version threshold, we will attempt to support backwards compatibility beyond two versions until the maintainers feel the maintenance burden is too high to continue doing so.

tip

For a canonical list of breaking changes, see the [Breaking Changes](/docs/latest/breaking-changes) document.

1: # Privacy sweep evidence
2: 
3: This directory holds the machine-readable output of the Phase 5 privacy gate:
4: `report.json`, produced by `scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs`.
5: 
6: **The repository is still private. No public flip has happened.** This is gate
7: evidence *for* a future flip, not a clearance and not an authorisation. Whoever
8: flips it should re-run the sweep at the release commit and commit the new
9: report; a report taken at an older commit says nothing about the one being
10: published.
11: 
12: ## Reproduce it
13: 
14: ```
15: node scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs --json docs/evidence/privacy/report.json
16: ```
17: 
18: Exit code 0 means the gate passed. Add `--no-history` for the working-tree leg
19: only (or `AGENT_DECK_SWEEP_HISTORY=0`), `--root <dir>` to sweep some other tree,
20: `--stamp <iso>` to fix the timestamp. The suite that asserts the same properties
21: is `src/release/privacy.test.ts`:
22: 
23: ```
24: npx vitest run src/release/privacy.test.ts
25: ```
26: 
27: The script reads only. Its single write is the file named by `--json`.
28: 
29: ## What it sweeps
30: 
31: Two corpora, both of them required by the DoD's phrase "full-history sweep":
32: 
33: 1. **the working tree** — every *tracked* file, enumerated with `git ls-files -z`
34:    so ignored build artifacts and `node_modules` are out of scope by
35:    construction rather than by hope;
36: 2. **history** — every blob reachable from **every ref**
37:    (`git rev-list --all --objects` piped into `git cat-file --batch`).
38: 
39: Both are scanned as **bytes in Node**, decoded `latin1` so one byte is one
40: character. That is not a stylistic preference. `src/parser/parse.test.ts`
41: contains real NUL bytes as deliberate fuzz input, and GNU `grep` without `-a`
42: abandons such a stream and returns a clean-looking, meaningless result. The
43: suite asserts that this file appears in the report's `nulFiles`, and a negative
44: control plants a marker behind 1000 NUL bytes and asserts the scanner still
45: finds it.
46: 
47: The sweep looks for the **developer identifier**, not for a path shape. This
48: matters more than it sounds: `webview/wire/cc-2.1.234-session-arc.json` stores
49: its Windows paths **double-escaped** in the JSON bytes, so a `grep 'C:\Users'`
50: returns zero on the file with the most absolute paths in the repository, while
51: forward-slash `c:/Users/…` forms sit in recorded `Bash` payloads. Searching for
52: the name and letting the path form fall out is what finds both.
53: 
54: Because history spans **every ref**, its totals include branches that are not
55: merged yet, and they move as a phase progresses. That is why the suite asserts
56: emptiness and structure and never a hit count.
57: 
58: ## The buckets
59: 
60: | bucket | meaning | gate |
61: | --- | --- | --- |
62: | `ALLOWED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by one of the enumerated allow rules, each of which carries a written reason | inventoried, not zeroed |
63: | `UNEXPECTED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by **no** allow rule | must be 0 |
64: | `SECRET` | a credential-shaped match: Anthropic key, GitHub token or PAT, AWS access key id, PEM private-key header, `Authorization: Bearer`, or a high-entropy value assigned to a key named like `token`/`secret`/`password`/`api_key` | must be 0 |
65: | `FOREIGN` | inside the enumerated corpora — since Phase 6, **every tracked top-level directory plus the root files** — a `cwd` / `transcript_path` / `agent_transcript_path` / project-slug value naming a project other than `agent-deck` | must be 0 |
66: | `ADVISORY` | an `ALLOWED` hit whose enclosing path points somewhere on the developer's own machine **outside** the agent-deck tree, `~/.claude` and `~/.vscode` | non-gating, listed by file and line |
67: 
68: A matched secret's **value is never printed** — only its location, its rule, and
69: a redacted shape (`abcd…<n chars redacted>…wxyz`). A negative control asserts
70: the planted secret string does not appear anywhere in the serialised report.
71: 
72: ## What the `FOREIGN` gate covers, and what it still does not (Phase 6)
73: 
74: Through Phase 5 the `FOREIGN` scan ran only inside an **eight-entry list of the
75: real-capture directories**, and `inCaptureCorpus()` gated the whole scan on it.
76: A tracked file anywhere else was never scanned for another project's content at
77: all. The Phase 5 verifier measured the hole rather than inferring it:
78: byte-identical foreign content planted at `src/model/leak.test.ts` and
79: `docs/notes.md` produced **zero** gate hits, while the same bytes under
80: `fixtures/hook-events/` produced **3**. This repository's own Phase 1 privacy
81: leak lived largely in **documents** — exactly the class that was outside the
82: gate.
83: 
84: Phase 6 **extended** the list to every tracked top-level directory plus the root
85: files. Extension, not inversion, was the user's decision at the gate, taken with
86: this consequence explicitly on record:
87: 
88: > **it is still an inclusion list.** A tracked top-level directory that nobody
89: > adds to `CAPTURE_CORPORA` is still outside the `FOREIGN` gate, and nothing
90: > about a default-deny scan protects it. "The `FOREIGN` gate is an inclusion
91: > list" therefore remains an open carry-out.
92: 
93: The mitigation is a **completeness guard**, which is what makes an inclusion
94: list survivable rather than merely smaller. `src/release/privacy.test.ts`
95: derives the set of tracked top-level directories from `git ls-files` **at test
96: time** — no count is written down, in this file or in the test — and fails when
97: any of them is not covered by an enumerated prefix. It also fails in the other
98: direction, on an enumerated prefix that matches no tracked file, so a typo
99: cannot look like coverage. Adding a new top-level directory without enumerating
100: it is a **red test**, not a silent hole.
101: 
102: Two things the guard does not do, said plainly: it says nothing about coverage
103: *within* a directory (a longer prefix such as `docs/evidence/` is rejected
104: precisely because partial coverage is the hole), and it cannot see an untracked
105: file, because the whole sweep is scoped to `git ls-files` by construction.
106: 
107: ### The exemptions, and the number they were measured against
108: 
109: Widening the corpora means the scan now reads source and prose that were never

1: # Agent Deck for Claude Code — Project Specification (v2)
2: 
3: **Marketplace ID:** `nvitlam.agent-deck` · **Display name:** Agent Deck for Claude Code
4: **Status:** Phase 1 closed **PASS** 9/9 (2026-08-19); Phase 0 closed **GO**. This spec v2 supersedes v1 in full; v1 is archived in `docs/`.
5: **Amendment rule:** documents win over chat until explicitly amended; amendments land in this spec first, then PLAN.md.
6: **Amended 2026-08-21 (Phase 4.5 gate — Canvas UI):** §5 C7 rewritten as the three-altitude canvas and given the normative visual-grammar state matrix; §6 records that the wire contract is unchanged by it; §7 and §9 brought into agreement with it; §8 gains three canvas rows. Design authority: `docs/ui/ui-canvas-redesign.md` and `docs/ui/agent-deck-canvas-mockup.html` — frozen under `spike/` rules, cited by path, never edited.
7: 
8: ---
9: 
10: ## 1. What this is
11: 
12: A **read-only VS Code extension** that live-visualizes Claude Code multi-agent sessions: subagent trees, tool calls in flight, token burn, cumulative cost. It observes CC's exhaust only — session files under `~/.claude/projects/` and user-installed hooks POSTing to a loopback listener. It never wraps, proxies, launches, or modifies Claude Code.
13: 
14: **Positioning:** live agent-swarm observability. The post-hoc space (ccusage, claude-code-log, opcode, Anthropic's official extension) is explicitly not the lane.
15: 
16: **Trust anchor:** read-only by design. No write capability in code, permissions, or marketing copy — ever.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 2. What Phase 0 proved (and disproved)
21: 
22: The v1 spec assumed subagent activity arrives as interleaved `"isSidechain":true` entries inside the main transcript, and called reconstructing trees from that interleaving "the core engineering problem."
23: 
24: **That premise was false.** Evidence (`fixtures/PHASE0-VERDICT.md`, adversarially verified, reproducible from a clean checkout): on the pinned CC version, main transcripts contain **zero** sidechain entries and **zero** `Task` tool calls. The spawning tool is **`Agent`**. Subagents are written as **separate files** with a metadata sidecar:
25: 
26: ```
27: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>.jsonl                                 main transcript
28: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl       subagent transcript (isSidechain:true, agentId)
29: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.meta.json   {agentType, description, toolUseId, spawnDepth, parentAgentId?}
30: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/tool-results/<id>.txt                 offloaded large tool payloads
31: ```
32: 
33: `meta.toolUseId` names the exact parent `tool_use` block; `spawnDepth` gives nesting level; `parentAgentId` appears at depth ≥ 2. **Attribution is a primary-key join, not an inference.** 27/27 agent transcripts resolved across four sessions with zero ambiguity.
34: 
35: Consequences encoded throughout this spec:
36: 
37: - "Tree stitching" is replaced by **tree grafting**: join subagent files onto parent `tool_use` nodes by `meta.toolUseId`.
38: - The product risk **moved**: nothing depends on interleaving semantics anymore; everything depends on the **undocumented directory-layout convention**. The schema fingerprint therefore asserts the *layout* (file naming, sidecar presence, join-key fields), not merely per-line field names.
39: - Discovery trap: `<slug>/memory/` sits as a sibling of `<sessionId>/` directories. Discovery must start from `<sessionId>.jsonl` **files** and only then look for the matching directory — never enumerate slug subdirectories as sessions. (The spike got this right; the production port must preserve the ordering.)
40: - Large tool payloads may live **outside** the JSONL in `tool-results/*.txt`. Redaction/truncation covers that path or previews silently miss content.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 3. Observation model
45: 
46: Two taps, two roles, failure-isolated:
47: 
48: | Source | Role | Contract status | Failure behavior |
49: |---|---|---|---|
50: | Hook events → loopback HTTP listener | **Liveness** (what is running right now) | Documented by Anthropic | Hooks absent → degraded mode (mtime + Stop-entry inference), non-nagging banner |
51: | Session files (JSONL + sidecars) | **Content** (tree, tool calls, tokens, cost) | Undocumented; pinned by fixtures | Fingerprint mismatch → session renders `unsupported`, never a partial tree |
52: 
53: A JSONL/layout parse failure must never take down liveness rendering (G2).
54: 
55: ### Hook payload facts (measured, 181 real events)
56: 
57: - Payload keys on real events match the documented contract and include the join keys `session_id`, `agent_id`, `tool_use_id`, plus `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`.

59: - Event types received from real CC on the pinned version: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop` — **all six confirmed** as of Phase 2.
60: - **`SessionStart` was confirmed last**, and only after a listener was bound *before* a fresh session opened (recipe R3). It fires at session onset, so every capture taken by a mid-session listener necessarily missed it; the absence measured bind order, not CC. Its payload is the smallest of any event (`session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `source`) and uniquely omits `prompt_id`. Liveness must still not *require* it.
61: - **`SubagentStart` was confirmed in Phase 2** (3/3 events, pinned in `fixtures/hook-events/`). 63: - Further undocumented keys observed on real events: `prompt_id`, `effort`, `permission_mode`, `duration_ms`, `background_tasks`, `session_crons`, `last_assistant_message`. Consumers preserve unknown keys and never reject on them.
64: - Hook installation is **manual**: a copy-paste block in the README targeting the user's settings. The extension never writes hook configuration. During development the block lives in the repo-local `.claude/settings.local.json`, installed by the human.

2: 
3: **Marketplace ID:** `nvitlam.agent-deck` · **Display name:** Agent Deck for Claude Code

5: **Amendment rule:** documents win over chat until explicitly amended; amendments land in this spec first, then PLAN.md.
6: **Amended 2026-08-21 (Phase 4.5 gate — Canvas UI):** §5 C7 rewritten as the three-altitude canvas and given the normative visual-grammar state matrix; §6 records that the wire contract is unchanged by it; §7 and §9 brought into agreement with it; §8 gains three canvas rows. 7: 
8: ---
9: 
10: ## 1. What this is
11: 
12: A **read-only VS Code extension** that live-visualizes Claude Code multi-agent sessions: subagent trees, tool calls in flight, token burn, cumulative cost. It observes CC's exhaust only — session files under `~/.claude/projects/` and user-installed hooks POSTing to a loopback listener. It never wraps, proxies, launches, or modifies Claude Code.
13: 
14: **Positioning:** live agent-swarm observability. The post-hoc space (ccusage, claude-code-log, opcode, Anthropic's official extension) is explicitly not the lane.
15: 
16: **Trust anchor:** read-only by design. No write capability in code, permissions, or marketing copy — ever.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 2. What Phase 0 proved (and disproved)
21: 
22: The v1 spec assumed subagent activity arrives as interleaved `"isSidechain":true` entries inside the main transcript, and called reconstructing trees from that interleaving "the core engineering problem."
23: 
24: **That premise was false.** Evidence (`fixtures/PHASE0-VERDICT.md`, adversarially verified, reproducible from a clean checkout): on the pinned CC version, main transcripts contain **zero** sidechain entries and **zero** `Task` tool calls. The spawning tool is **`Agent`**. Subagents are written as **separate files** with a metadata sidecar:
25: 
26: ```
27: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>.jsonl                                 main transcript
28: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl       subagent transcript (isSidechain:true, agentId)
29: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.meta.json   {agentType, description, toolUseId, spawnDepth, parentAgentId?}
30: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/tool-results/<id>.txt                 offloaded large tool payloads
31: ```
32: 
33: `meta.toolUseId` names the exact parent `tool_use` block; `spawnDepth` gives nesting level; `parentAgentId` appears at depth ≥ 2. **Attribution is a primary-key join, not an inference.** 27/27 agent transcripts resolved across four sessions with zero ambiguity.
34: 
35: Consequences encoded throughout this spec:
36: 
37: - "Tree stitching" is replaced by **tree grafting**: join subagent files onto parent `tool_use` nodes by `meta.toolUseId`.
38: - The product risk **moved**: nothing depends on interleaving semantics anymore; everything depends on the **undocumented directory-layout convention**. The schema fingerprint therefore asserts the *layout* (file naming, sidecar presence, join-key fields), not merely per-line field names.
39: - Discovery trap: `<slug>/memory/` sits as a sibling of `<sessionId>/` directories. Discovery must start from `<sessionId>.jsonl` **files** and only then look for the matching directory — never enumerate slug subdirectories as sessions. (The spike got this right; the production port must preserve the ordering.)
40: - Large tool payloads may live **outside** the JSONL in `tool-results/*.txt`. Redaction/truncation covers that path or previews silently miss content.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 3. Observation model
45: 
46: Two taps, two roles, failure-isolated:
47: 
48: | Source | Role | Contract status | Failure behavior |
49: |---|---|---|---|
50: | Hook events → loopback HTTP listener | **Liveness** (what is running right now) | Documented by Anthropic | Hooks absent → degraded mode (mtime + Stop-entry inference), non-nagging banner |
51: | Session files (JSONL + sidecars) | **Content** (tree, tool calls, tokens, cost) | Undocumented; pinned by fixtures | Fingerprint mismatch → session renders `unsupported`, never a partial tree |
52: 
53: A JSONL/layout parse failure must never take down liveness rendering (G2).
54: 
55: ### Hook payload facts (measured, 181 real events)
56: 
57: - Payload keys on real events match the documented contract and include the join keys `session_id`, `agent_id`, `tool_use_id`, plus `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`.
58: - **Main-thread events carry no `agent_id` key at all.** CC omits the field; the literal `"main"` appeared in 0/181 events. *Absence of the key is the main-thread signal.* Any correlator matching a `"main"` string silently drops every main-thread event.
59: - Event types received from real CC on the pinned version: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop` — **all six confirmed** as of Phase 2.
60: - **`SessionStart` was confirmed last**, and only after a listener was bound *before* a fresh session opened (recipe R3). It fires at session onset, so every capture taken by a mid-session listener necessarily missed it; the absence measured bind order, not CC. Its payload is the smallest of any event (`session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `source`) and uniquely omits `prompt_id`. Liveness must still not *require* it.
61: - **`SubagentStart` was confirmed in Phase 2** (3/3 events, pinned in `fixtures/hook-events/`). It carries `agent_id` and `agent_type` but **no `tool_use_id`**, so it cannot by itself attribute a subagent to its spawning `tool_use` block.
62: - **`SubagentStop` carries `agent_transcript_path`**, resolving to `<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl`. The undocumented directory layout (§2) is therefore corroborated by the *documented* hook contract — the top risk in §8 gains an independent witness.
63: - Further undocumented keys observed on real events: `prompt_id`, `effort`, `permission_mode`, `duration_ms`, `background_tasks`, `session_crons`, `last_assistant_message`. Consumers preserve unknown keys and never reject on them.
64: - Hook installation is **manual**: a copy-paste block in the README targeting the user's settings. The extension never writes hook configuration. During development the block lives in the repo-local `.claude/settings.local.json`, installed by the human.
65:

The numbers live in that module and are deliberately not duplicated as literals anywhere that could go stale — this section names them once so a reader has them, and a release test asserts these words against those constants.

72: - **Anchor: `2.1.234`** — the version the committed capture under `fixtures/cc-2.1.234/` was taken from, and the only version whose behaviour is pinned byte-for-byte.
73: - **Window: major exact, minor +/-1, patch +/-5**, i.e. `2.0.229` to `2.2.239` around that anchor. It is a **box, not a lexicographic range**: each component must sit inside its own tolerance, so `2.2.100` falls between the corners and is sti

21:   written, created, or deleted.

28: %USERPROFILE%\.local\share\opencode\
29:   opencode.db        2,482,176 bytes at measurement   <- the only file the engine reads
30:   opencode.db-wal    4,161,232 bytes at measurement   WAL mode, live writer present

1: # Agent Deck for Claude Code — Project Specification (v2)
2: 
3: **Marketplace ID:** `nvitlam.agent-deck` · **Display name:** Agent Deck for Claude Code
4: **Status:** Phase 1 closed **PASS** 9/9 (2026-08-19); Phase 0 closed **GO**. This spec v2 supersedes v1 in full; v1 is archived in `docs/`.
5: **Amendment rule:** documents win over chat until explicitly amended; amendments land in this spec first, then PLAN.md.
6: **Amended 2026-08-21 (Phase 4.5 gate — Canvas UI):** §5 C7 rewritten as the three-altitude canvas and given the normative visual-grammar state matrix; §6 records that the wire contract is unchanged by it; §7 and §9 brought into agreement with it; §8 gains three canvas rows. Design authority: `docs/ui/ui-canvas-redesign.md` and `docs/ui/agent-deck-canvas-mockup.html` — frozen under `spike/` rules, cited by path, never edited.
7: 
8: ---
9: 
10: ## 1. What this is
11: 
12: A **read-only VS Code extension** that live-visualizes Claude Code multi-agent sessions: subagent trees, tool calls in flight, token burn, cumulative cost. It observes CC's exhaust only — session files under `~/.claude/projects/` and user-installed hooks POSTing to a loopback listener. It never wraps, proxies, launches, or modifies Claude Code.
13: 
14: **Positioning:** live agent-swarm observability. The post-hoc space (ccusage, claude-code-log, opcode, Anthropic's official extension) is explicitly not the lane.
15: 
16: **Trust anchor:** read-only by design. No write capability in code, permissions, or marketing copy — ever.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 2. What Phase 0 proved (and disproved)
21: 
22: The v1 spec assumed subagent activity arrives as interleaved `"isSidechain":true` entries inside the main transcript, and called reconstructing trees from that interleaving "the core engineering problem."
23: 
24: **That premise was false.** Evidence (`fixtures/PHASE0-VERDICT.md`, adversarially verified, reproducible from a clean checkout): on the pinned CC version, main transcripts contain **zero** sidechain entries and **zero** `Task` tool calls. The spawning tool is **`Agent`**. Subagents are written as **separate files** with a metadata sidecar:
25: 
26: ```
27: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>.jsonl                                 main transcript
28: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl       subagent transcript (isSidechain:true, agentId)
29: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.meta.json   {agentType, description, toolUseId, spawnDepth, parentAgentId?}
30: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/tool-results/<id>.txt                 offloaded large tool payloads
31: ```
32: 
33: `meta.toolUseId` names the exact parent `tool_use` block; `spawnDepth` gives nesting level; `parentAgentId` appears at depth ≥ 2. **Attribution is a primary-key join, not an inference.** 27/27 agent transcripts resolved across four sessions with zero ambiguity.
34: 
35: Consequences encoded throughout this spec:
36: 
37: - "Tree stitching" is replaced by **tree grafting**: join subagent files onto parent `tool_use` nodes by `meta.toolUseId`.
38: - The product risk **moved**: nothing depends on interleaving semantics anymore; everything depends on the **undocumented directory-layout convention**. The schema fingerprint therefore asserts the *layout* (file naming, sidecar presence, join-key fields), not merely per-line field names.
39: - Discovery trap: `<slug>/memory/` sits as a sibling of `<sessionId>/` directories. Discovery must start from `<sessionId>.jsonl` **files** and only then look for the matching directory — never enumerate slug subdirectories as sessions. (The spike got this right; the production port must preserve the ordering.)
40: - Large tool payloads may live **outside** the JSONL in `tool-results/*.txt`. Redaction/truncation covers that path or previews silently miss content.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 3. Observation model
45: 
46: Two taps, two roles, failure-isolated:

21:  *
22:  * READ-ONLY except for the report file named by `--json`. No network, no
23:  * dependencies outside `node:` builtins. It never mutates the repository, and
24:  * it never prints a matched secret value.
25:  *
26:  * WHAT IT SWEEPS
27:  * --------------
28:  * Two corpora:
29:  *   1. the working tree - every TRACKED file (`git ls-files -z`), so ignored
30:  *      build artifacts and `node_modules` are out of scope by construction;

32:  *      (`git rev-list --all --objects` + `git cat-file --batch`).

37:  * stream and returns a clean-looking, meaningless result. Scanning buffers
38:  * sidesteps grep's binary heuristic entirely. `latin1` is safe for the ASCII
39:  * needles used here because UTF-8 continuation bytes always have the high bit
40:  * set and can never collide with an ASCII pattern.
41:  *

47:  * main-thread hook rule and a normalised recording is not a recording of the
48:  * real wire. Deleting fixture content to make a counter reach zero would

50:  * paths is an ENUMERATED INVENTORY of a known set, plus zero outside it.

1: # Privacy sweep evidence
2: 
3: This directory holds the machine-readable output of the Phase 5 privacy gate:
4: `report.json`, produced by `scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs`.
5: 
6: **The repository is still private. No public flip has happened.** This is gate
7: evidence *for* a future flip, not a clearance and not an authorisation. Whoever
8: flips it should re-run the sweep at the release commit and commit the new
9: report; a report taken at an older commit says nothing about the one being
10: published.
11: 
12: ## Reproduce it
13: 
14: ```
15: node scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs --json docs/evidence/privacy/report.json
16: ```
17: 
18: Exit code 0 means the gate passed. Add `--no-history` for the working-tree leg
19: only (or `AGENT_DECK_SWEEP_HISTORY=0`), `--root <dir>` to sweep some other tree,
20: `--stamp <iso>` to fix the timestamp. The suite that asserts the same properties
21: is `src/release/privacy.test.ts`:
22: 
23: ```
24: npx vitest run src/release/privacy.test.ts
25: ```
26: 
27: The script reads only. Its single write is the file named by `--json`.
28: 
29: ## What it sweeps
30: 
31: Two corpora, both of them required by the DoD's phrase "full-history sweep":
32: 
33: 1. **the working tree** — every *tracked* file, enumerated with `git ls-files -z`
34:    so ignored build artifacts and `node_modules` are out of scope by
35:    construction rather than by hope;
36: 2. **history** — every blob reachable from **every ref**
37:    (`git rev-list --all --objects` piped into `git cat-file --batch`).
38: 
39: Both are scanned as **bytes in Node**, decoded `latin1` so one byte is one
40: character. That is not a stylistic preference. `src/parser/parse.test.ts`
41: contains real NUL bytes as deliberate fuzz input, and GNU `grep` without `-a`
42: abandons such a stream and returns a clean-looking, meaningless result. The
43: suite asserts that this file appears in the report's `nulFiles`, and a negative
44: control plants a marker behind 1000 NUL bytes and asserts the scanner still
45: finds it.
46: 
47: The sweep looks for the **developer identifier**, not for a path shape. This
48: matters more than it sounds: `webview/wire/cc-2.1.234-session-arc.json` stores
49: its Windows paths **double-escaped** in the JSON bytes, so a `grep 'C:\Users'`
50: returns zero on the file with the most absolute paths in the repository, while
51: forward-slash `c:/Users/…` forms sit in recorded `Bash` payloads. Searching for
52: the name and letting the path form fall out is what finds both.
53: 
54: Because history spans **every ref**, its totals include branches that are not
55: merged yet, and they move as a phase progresses. That is why the suite asserts
56: emptiness and structure and never a hit count.
57: 
58: ## The buckets
59: 
60: | bucket | meaning | gate |
61: | --- | --- | --- |
62: | `ALLOWED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by one of the enumerated allow rules, each of which carries a written reason | inventoried, not zeroed |
63: | `UNEXPECTED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by **no** allow rule | must be 0 |
64: | `SECRET` | a credential-shaped match: Anthropic key, GitHub token or PAT, AWS access key id, PEM private-key header, `Authorization: Bearer`, or a high-entropy value assigned to a key named like `token`/`secret`/`password`/`api_key` | must be 0 |
65: | `FOREIGN` | inside the enumerated corpora — since Phase 6, **every tracked top-level directory plus the root files** — a `cwd` / `transcript_path` / `agent_transcript_path` / project-slug value naming a project other than `agent-deck` | must be 0 |
66: | `ADVISORY` | an `ALLOWED` hit whose enclosing path points somewhere on the developer's own machine **outside** the agent-deck tree, `~/.claude` and `~/.vscode` | non-gating, listed by file and line |
67: 
68: A matched secret's **value is never printed** — only its location, its rule, and
69: a redacted shape (`abcd…<n chars redacted>…wxyz`). A negative control asserts
70: the planted secret string does not appear anywhere in the serialised report.
71: 
72: ## What the `FOREIGN` gate covers, and what it still does not (Phase 6)
73: 
74: Through Phase 5 the `FOREIGN` scan ran only inside an **eight-entry list of the
75: real-capture directories**, and `inCaptureCorpus()` gated the whole scan on it.
76: A tracked file anywhere else was never scanned for another project's content at
77: all. The Phase 5 verifier measured the hole rather than inferring it:
78: byte-identical foreign content planted at `src/model/leak.test.ts` and
79: `docs/notes.md` produced **zero** gate hits, while the same bytes under
80: `fixtures/hook-events/` produced **3**. This repository's own Phase 1 privacy
81: leak lived largely in **documents** — exactly the class that was outside the
82: gate.
83: 
84: Phase 6 **extended** the list to every tracked top-level directory plus the root
85: files. Extension, not inversion, was the user's decision at the gate, taken with
86: this consequence explicitly on record:
87: 
88: > **it is still an inclusion list.** A tracked top-level directory that nobody
89: > adds to `CAPTURE_CORPORA` is still outside the `FOREIGN` gate, and nothing
90: > about a default-deny scan protects it. "The `FOREIGN` gate is an inclusion
91: > list" therefore remains an open carry-out.
92: 
93: The mitigation is a **completeness guard**, which is what makes an inclusion
94: list survivable rather than merely smaller. `src/release/privacy.test.ts`
95: derives the set of tracked top-level directories from `git ls-files` **at test
96: time** — no count is written down, in this file or in the test — and fails when
97: any of them is not covered by an enumerated prefix. It also fails in the other
98: direction, on an enumerated prefix that matches no tracked file, so a typo
99: cannot look like coverage. Adding a new top-level directory without enumerating
100: it is a **red test**, not a silent hole.
101: 
102: Two things the guard does not do, said plainly: it says nothing about coverage
103: *within* a directory (a longer prefix such as `docs/evidence/` is rejected
104: precisely because partial coverage is the hole), and it cannot see an untracked
105: file, because the whole sweep is scoped to `git ls-files` by construction.
106: 
107: ### The exemptions, and the number they were measured against
108: 
109: Widening the corpora means the scan now reads source and prose that were never
110: in it. Measured on this repository at `b4f6c76` with the corpora widened and
111: **no exemption added at all** — the numbers below are that one historical
112: measurement, not live counters, and are not to be refreshed as the tree moves —
113: the gate reported `foreign=32` (8 working tree, 24 history). None of the 32
114: was content captured from another project. They were two shapes:
115: 
116: - **29** were one identical *source literal* — a regex that seven files carry in
117:   order to **parse** a hook payload, whose own text spells the key name, so the
118:   scanner captured the regex body instead of a path;
119: - **3** were the negative controls' own planted string, in the source of
120:   `src/release/privacy.test.ts` and its history, naming a project that does not
121:   exist.
122: 
123: The exemptions are keyed on the **value**, not on the path, and each carries a
124: written reason in `config.foreignValueExemptions` in the report. By value and
125: not by path deliberately: a path-shaped exemption blinds a whole directory,
126: which is the defect being closed here, not one to reintroduce a level down. The
127: one entry that *is* path-scoped names one exact file and one exact invented
128: value. Negative controls cover both directions — the planted copies under
129: `fixtures/`, `src/` and `docs/` must all still be flagged, and the regex literal
130: must not be.
131: 
132: ## Why `ALLOWED` is not zero, and why making it zero would be vandalism
133:

2: 
3: **Marketplace ID:** `nvitlam.agent-deck` · **Display name:** Agent Deck for Claude Code

5: **Amendment rule:** documents win over chat until explicitly amended; amendments land in this spec first, then PLAN.md.

7: 
8: ---
9: 
10: ## 1. What this is
11: 
12: A **read-only VS Code extension** that live-visualizes Claude Code multi-agent sessions: subagent trees, tool calls in flight, token burn, cumulative cost. It observes CC's exhaust only — session files under `~/.claude/projects/` and user-installed hooks POSTing to a loopback listener. It never wraps, proxies, launches, or modifies Claude Code.
13: 
14: **Positioning:** live agent-swarm observability. The post-hoc space (ccusage, claude-code-log, opcode, Anthropic's official extension) is explicitly not the lane.
15: 
16: **Trust anchor:** read-only by design. No write capability in code, permissions, or marketing copy — ever.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 2. What Phase 0 proved (and disproved)
21: 
22: The v1 spec assumed subagent activity arrives as interleaved `"isSidechain":true` entries inside the main transcript, and called reconstructing trees from that interleaving "the core engineering problem."
23: 
24: **That premise was false.** Evidence (`fixtures/PHASE0-VERDICT.md`, adversarially verified, reproducible from a clean checkout): on the pinned CC version, main transcripts contain **zero** sidechain entries and **zero** `Task` tool calls. The spawning tool is **`Agent`**. Subagents are written as **separate files** with a metadata sidecar:
25: 
26: ```
27: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>.jsonl                                 main transcript
28: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl       subagent transcript (isSidechain:true, agentId)
29: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.meta.json   {agentType, description, toolUseId, spawnDepth, parentAgentId?}
30: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/tool-results/<id>.txt                 offloaded large tool payloads
31: ```
32: 
33: `meta.toolUseId` names the exact parent `tool_use` block; `spawnDepth` gives nesting level; `parentAgentId` appears at depth ≥ 2. **Attribution is a primary-key join, not an inference.** 27/27 agent transcripts resolved across four sessions with zero ambiguity.
34: 
35: Consequences encoded throughout this spec:
36: 
37: - "Tree stitching" is replaced by **tree grafting**: join subagent files onto parent `tool_use` nodes by `meta.toolUseId`.
38: - The product risk **moved**: nothing depends on interleaving semantics anymore; everything depends on the **undocumented directory-layout convention**. The schema fingerprint therefore asserts the *layout* (file naming, sidecar presence, join-key fields), not merely per-line field names.
39: - Discovery trap: `<slug>/memory/` sits as a sibling of `<sessionId>/` directories. Discovery must start from `<sessionId>.jsonl` **files** and only then look for the matching directory — never enumerate slug subdirectories as sessions. (The spike got this right; the production port must preserve the ordering.)
40: - Large tool payloads may live **outside** the JSONL in `tool-results/*.txt`. Redaction/truncation covers that path or previews silently miss content.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 3. Observation model
45: 
46: Two taps, two roles, failure-isolated:
47: 
48: | Source | Role | Contract status | Failure behavior |
49: |---|---|---|---|
50: | Hook events → loopback HTTP listener | **Liveness** (what is running right now) | Documented by Anthropic | Hooks absent → degraded mode (mtime + Stop-entry inference), non-nagging banner |
51: | Session files (JSONL + sidecars) | **Content** (tree, tool calls, tokens, cost) | Undocumented; pinned by fixtures | Fingerprint mismatch → session renders `unsupported`, never a partial tree |
52: 
53: A JSONL/layout parse failure must never take down liveness rendering (G2).
54: 
55: ### Hook payload facts (measured, 181 real events)
56: 
57: - Payload keys on real events match the documented contract and include the join keys `session_id`, `agent_id`, `tool_use_id`, plus `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `tool_name`, `tool_input`.
58: - **Main-thread events carry no `agent_id` key at all.** CC omits the field; the literal `"main"` appeared in 0/181 events. *Absence of the key is the main-thread signal.* Any correlator matching a `"main"` string silently drops every main-thread event.
59: - Event types received from real CC on the pinned version: `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop` — **all six confirmed** as of Phase 2.
60: - **`SessionStart` was confirmed last**, and only after a listener was bound *before* a fresh session opened (recipe R3). It fires at session onset, so every capture taken by a mid-session listener necessarily missed it; the absence measured bind order, not CC. Its payload is the smallest of any event (`session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `source`) and uniquely omits `prompt_id`. Liveness must still not *require* it.
61: - **`SubagentStart` was confirmed in Phase 2** (3/3 events, pinned in `fixtures/hook-events/`). It had previously been dismissed as "a string in the CC binary, never observed" — but it had never been *registered* in the hook block, so the absence measured our configuration rather than CC. It carries `agent_id` and `agent_type` but **no `tool_use_id`**, so it cannot by itself attribute a subagent to its spawning `tool_use` block.
62: - **`SubagentStop` carries `agent_transcript_path`**, resolving to `<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl`. The undocumented directory layout (§2) is therefore corroborated by the *documented* hook contract — the top risk in §8 gains an independent witness.
63: - Further undocumented keys observed on real events: `prompt_id`, `effort`, `permission_mode`, `duration_ms`, `background_tasks`, `session_crons`, `last_assistant_message`. Consumers preserve unknown keys and never reject on them.
64: - Hook installation is **manual**: a copy-paste block in the README targeting the user's settings. The extension never writes hook configuration. During development the block lives in the repo-local `.claude/settings.local.json`, installed by the human.
65: 
66: ### Version posture
67:

73: - **Window: major exact, minor +/-1, patch +/-5**, i.e. `2.0.229` to `2.2.239` around that anchor. It is a **box, not a lexicographic range**: each component must sit inside its own tolerance, so `2.2.100` falls between the corners and is sti

1: # Privacy sweep evidence
2: 
3: This directory holds the machine-readable output of the Phase 5 privacy gate:
4: `report.json`, produced by `scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs`.
5: 
6: **The repository is still private. No public flip has happened.** This is gate
7: evidence *for* a future flip, not a clearance and not an authorisation. Whoever
8: flips it should re-run the sweep at the release commit and commit the new
9: report; a report taken at an older commit says nothing about the one being
10: published.
11: 
12: ## Reproduce it
13: 
14: ```
15: node scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs --json docs/evidence/privacy/report.json
16: ```
17: 
18: Exit code 0 means the gate passed. Add `--no-history` for the working-tree leg
19: only (or `AGENT_DECK_SWEEP_HISTORY=0`), `--root <dir>` to sweep some other tree,
20: `--stamp <iso>` to fix the timestamp. The suite that asserts the same properties
21: is `src/release/privacy.test.ts`:
22: 
23: ```
24: npx vitest run src/release/privacy.test.ts
25: ```
26: 
27: The script reads only. Its single write is the file named by `--json`.
28: 
29: ## What it sweeps
30: 
31: Two corpora, both of them required by the DoD's phrase "full-history sweep":
32: 
33: 1. **the working tree** — every *tracked* file, enumerated with `git ls-files -z`
34:    so ignored build artifacts and `node_modules` are out of scope by
35:    construction rather than by hope;
36: 2. **history** — every blob reachable from **every ref**
37:    (`git rev-list --all --objects` piped into `git cat-file --batch`).
38: 
39: Both are scanned as **bytes in Node**, decoded `latin1` so one byte is one
40: character. That is not a stylistic preference. `src/parser/parse.test.ts`
41: contains real NUL bytes as deliberate fuzz input, and GNU `grep` without `-a`
42: abandons such a stream and returns a clean-looking, meaningless result. The
43: suite asserts that this file appears in the report's `nulFiles`, and a negative
44: control plants a marker behind 1000 NUL bytes and asserts the scanner still
45: finds it.
46: 
47: The sweep looks for the **developer identifier**, not for a path shape. This
48: matters more than it sounds: `webview/wire/cc-2.1.234-session-arc.json` stores
49: its Windows paths **double-escaped** in the JSON bytes, so a `grep 'C:\Users'`
50: returns zero on the file with the most absolute paths in the repository, while
51: forward-slash `c:/Users/…` forms sit in recorded `Bash` payloads. Searching for
52: the name and letting the path form fall out is what finds both.
53: 
54: Because history spans **every ref**, its totals include branches that are not
55: merged yet, and they move as a phase progresses. That is why the suite asserts
56: emptiness and structure and never a hit count.
57: 
58: ## The buckets
59: 
60: | bucket | meaning | gate |
61: | --- | --- | --- |
62: | `ALLOWED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by one of the enumerated allow rules, each of which carries a written reason | inventoried, not zeroed |
63: | `UNEXPECTED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by **no** allow rule | must be 0 |
64: | `SECRET` | a credential-shaped match: Anthropic key, GitHub token or PAT, AWS access key id, PEM private-key header, `Authorization: Bearer`, or a high-entropy value assigned to a key named like `token`/`secret`/`password`/`api_key` | must be 0 |
65: | `FOREIGN` | inside the enumerated corpora — since Phase 6, **every tracked top-level directory plus the root files** — a `cwd` / `transcript_path` / `agent_transcript_path` / project-slug value naming a project other than `agent-deck` | must be 0 |
66: | `ADVISORY` | an `ALLOWED` hit whose enclosing path points somewhere on the developer's own machine **outside** the agent-deck tree, `~/.claude` and `~/.vscode` | non-gating, listed by file and line |
67: 
68: A matched secret's **value is never printed** — only its location, its rule, and
69: a redacted shape (`abcd…<n chars redacted>…wxyz`). A negative control asserts
70: the planted secret string does not appear anywhere in the serialised report.
71: 
72: ## What the `FOREIGN` gate covers, and what it still does not (Phase 6)
73: 
74: Through Phase 5 the `FOREIGN` scan ran only inside an **eight-entry list of the
75: real-capture directories**, and `inCaptureCorpus()` gated the whole scan on it.
76: A tracked file anywhere else was never scanned for another project's content at
77: all. The Phase 5 verifier measured the hole rather than inferring it:
78: byte-identical foreign content planted at `src/model/leak.test.ts` and
79: `docs/notes.md` produced **zero** gate hits, while the same bytes under
80: `fixtures/hook-events/` produced **3**. This repository's own Phase 1 privacy
81: leak lived largely in **documents** — exactly the class that was outside the
82: gate.
83: 
84: Phase 6 **extended** the list to every tracked top-level directory plus the root
85: files. Extension, not inversion, was the user's decision at the gate, taken with
86: this consequence explicitly on record:
87: 
88: > **it is still an inclusion list.** A tracked top-level directory that nobody
89: > adds to `CAPTURE_CORPORA` is still outside the `FOREIGN` gate, and nothing
90: > about a default-deny scan protects it. "The `FOREIGN` gate is an inclusion
91: > list" therefore remains an open carry-out.
92: 
93: The mitigation is a **completeness guard**, which is what makes an inclusion
94: list survivable rather than merely smaller. `src/release/privacy.test.ts`
95: derives the set of tracked top-level directories from `git ls-files` **at test
96: time** — no count is written down, in this file or in the test — and fails when
97: any of them is not covered by an enumerated prefix. It also fails in the other
98: direction, on an enumerated prefix that matches no tracked file, so a typo
99: cannot look like coverage. Adding a new top-level directory without enumerating
100: it is a **red test**, not a silent hole.
101: 
102: Two things the guard does not do, said plainly: it says nothing about coverage
103: *within* a directory (a longer prefix such as `docs/evidence/` is rejected
104: precisely because partial coverage is the hole), and it cannot see an untracked
105: file, because the whole sweep is scoped to `git ls-files` by construction.
106: 
107: ### The exemptions, and the number they were measured against
108: 
109: Widening the corpora means the scan now reads source and prose that were never
110: in it. Measured on this repository at `b4f6c76` with the corpora widened and
111: **no exemption added at all** — the numbers below are that one historical
112: measurement, not live counters, and are not to be refreshed as the tree moves —
113: the gate reported `foreign=32` (8 working tree, 24 history). None of the 32
114: was content captured from another project. They were two shapes:

14: **Positioning:** live agent-swarm observability. The post-hoc space (ccusage, claude-code-log, opcode, Anthropic's official extension) is explicitly not the lane.

16: **Trust anchor:** read-only by design. No write capability in code, permissions, or marketing copy — ever.

20: ## 2. What Phase 0 proved (and disproved)
21: 
22: The v1 spec assumed subagent activity arrives as interleaved `"isSidechain":true` entries inside the main transcript, and called reconstructing trees from that interleaving "the core engineering problem."
23: 
24: **That premise was false.** Evidence (`fixtures/PHASE0-VERDICT.md`, adversarially verified, reproducible from a clean checkout): on the pinned CC version, main transcripts contain **zero** sidechain entries and **zero** `Task` tool calls. The spawning tool is **`Agent`**. Subagents are written as **separate files** with a metadata sidecar:
25: 
26: ```
27: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>.jsonl                                 main transcript
28: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl       subagent transcript (isSidechain:true, agentId)
29: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.meta.json   {agentType, description, toolUseId, spawnDepth, parentAgentId?}
30: projects/<slug>/<sessionId>/tool-results/<id>.txt                 offloaded large tool payloads
31: ```
32: 
33: `meta.toolUseId` names the exact parent `tool_use` block; `spawnDepth` gives nesting level; `parentAgentId` appears at depth ≥ 2. **Attribution is a primary-key join, not an inference.** 27/27 agent transcripts resolved across four sessions with zero ambiguity.
34:

38: - The product risk **moved**: nothing depends on interleaving semantics anymore; everything depends on the **undocumented directory-layout convention**. The schema fingerprint therefore asserts the *layout* (file naming, sidecar presence, join-key fields), not merely per-line field names.
39: - Discovery trap: `<slug>/memory/` sits as a sibling of `<sessionId>/` directories. Discovery must start from `<sessionId>.jsonl` **files** and only then look for the matching directory — never enumerate slug subdirectories as sessions. (The spike got this right; the production port must preserve the ordering.)
40: - Large tool payloads may live **outside** the JSONL in `tool-results/*.txt`. Redaction/truncation covers that path or previews silently miss content.
41:

1: # Privacy sweep evidence
2: 
3: This directory holds the machine-readable output of the Phase 5 privacy gate:
4: `report.json`, produced by `scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs`.
5: 
6: **The repository is still private. No public flip has happened.** This is gate
7: evidence *for* a future flip, not a clearance and not an authorisation. Whoever
8: flips it should re-run the sweep at the release commit and commit the new
9: report; a report taken at an older commit says nothing about the one being
10: published.
11: 
12: ## Reproduce it
13: 
14: ```
15: node scripts/privacy-sweep.mjs --json docs/evidence/privacy/report.json
16: ```
17: 
18: Exit code 0 means the gate passed. Add `--no-history` for the working-tree leg
19: only (or `AGENT_DECK_SWEEP_HISTORY=0`), `--root <dir>` to sweep some other tree,
20: `--stamp <iso>` to fix the timestamp. The suite that asserts the same properties
21: is `src/release/privacy.test.ts`:
22: 
23: ```
24: npx vitest run src/release/privacy.test.ts
25: ```
26: 
27: The script reads only. Its single write is the file named by `--json`.
28: 
29: ## What it sweeps
30: 
31: Two corpora, both of them required by the DoD's phrase "full-history sweep":
32: 
33: 1. **the working tree** — every *tracked* file, enumerated with `git ls-files -z`
34:    so ignored build artifacts and `node_modules` are out of scope by
35:    construction rather than by hope;
36: 2. **history** — every blob reachable from **every ref**
37:    (`git rev-list --all --objects` piped into `git cat-file --batch`).
38: 
39: Both are scanned as **bytes in Node**, decoded `latin1` so one byte is one
40: character. That is not a stylistic preference. `src/parser/parse.test.ts`
41: contains real NUL bytes as deliberate fuzz input, and GNU `grep` without `-a`
42: abandons such a stream and returns a clean-looking, meaningless result. The
43: suite asserts that this file appears in the report's `nulFiles`, and a negative
44: control plants a marker behind 1000 NUL bytes and asserts the scanner still
45: finds it.
46: 
47: The sweep looks for the **developer identifier**, not for a path shape. This
48: matters more than it sounds: `webview/wire/cc-2.1.234-session-arc.json` stores
49: its Windows paths **double-escaped** in the JSON bytes, so a `grep 'C:\Users'`
50: returns zero on the file with the most absolute paths in the repository, while
51: forward-slash `c:/Users/…` forms sit in recorded `Bash` payloads. Searching for
52: the name and letting the path form fall out is what finds both.
53: 
54: Because history spans **every ref**, its totals include branches that are not
55: merged yet, and they move as a phase progresses. That is why the suite asserts
56: emptiness and structure and never a hit count.
57: 
58: ## The buckets
59: 
60: | bucket | meaning | gate |
61: | --- | --- | --- |
62: | `ALLOWED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by one of the enumerated allow rules, each of which carries a written reason | inventoried, not zeroed |
63: | `UNEXPECTED` | a developer-identifier hit in a file matched by **no** allow rule | must be 0 |
64: | `SECRET` | a credential-shaped match: Anthropic key, GitHub token or PAT, AWS access key id, PEM private-key header, `Authorization: Bearer`, or a high-entropy value assigned to a key named like `token`/`secret`/`password`/`api_key` | must be 0 |
65: | `FOREIGN` | inside the enumerated corpora — since Phase 6, **every tracked top-level directory plus the root files** — a `cwd` / `transcript_path` / `agent_transcript_path` / project-slug value naming a project other than `agent-deck` | must be 0 |
66: | `ADVISORY` | an `ALLOWED` hit whose enclosing path points somewhere on the developer's own machine **outside** the agent-deck tree, `~/.claude` and `~/.vscode` | non-gating, listed by file and line |
67: 
68: A matched secret's **value is never printed** — only its location, its rule, and
69: a redacted shape (`abcd…<n chars redacted>…wxyz`). A negative control asserts
70: the planted secret string does not appear anywhere in the serialised report.
71: 
72: ## What the `FOREIGN` gate covers, and what it still does not (Phase 6)
73: 
74: Through Phase 5 the `FOREIGN` scan ran only inside an **eight-entry list of the
75: real-capture directories**, and `inCaptureCorpus()` gated the whole scan on it.
76: A tracked file anywhere else was never scanned for another project's content at
77: all. The Phase 5 verifier measured the hole rather than inferring it:
78: byte-identical foreign content planted at `src/model/leak.test.ts` and
79: `docs/notes.md` produced **zero** gate hits, while the same bytes under
80: `fixtures/hook-events/` produced **3**. This repository's own Phase 1 privacy
81: leak lived largely in **documents** — exactly the class that was outside the
82: gate.
83: 
84: Phase 6 **extended** the list to every tracked top-level directory plus the root
85: files. Extension, not inversion, was the user's decision at the gate, taken with
86: this consequence explicitly on record:
87: 
88: > **it is still an inclusion list.** A tracked top-level directory that nobody
89: > adds to `CAPTURE_CORPORA` is still outside the `FOREIGN` gate, and nothing
90: > about a default-deny scan protects it. "The `FOREIGN` gate is an inclusion
91: > list" therefore remains an open carry-out.
92: 
93: The mitigation is a **completeness guard**, which is what makes an inclusion
